title: Rome’s bronze she-wolf, long called Etruscan, may have been cast in the Middle Ages
body: The she-wolf in the Capitoline Museums, who in the legend fed Romulus and Remus, was long dated to the 5th century BC as an Etruscan work; the twins under her were added in the late 15th century, probably by the sculptor Antonio del Pollaiuolo. While restoring her in 1997–2000, Anna Maria Carruba found she had been cast in a single piece by the lost-wax method, as bells were in the Middle Ages, while large ancient bronzes were cast in parts and joined. The clay core left inside her held two clocks. Radiocarbon dating of 34 organic samples from it, at the University of Salento, gave AD 1021–1153; [thermoluminescence](https://boa.unimib.it/retrieve/9f5fadfe-d0e4-4728-9b55-7f1c12863cb0/10281-324556_VoR.pdf) of the clay, which measures the radiation dose stored since the casting heated it, is less precise but puts the casting between the 8th and 14th centuries. Many scholars still disagree: at a conference in Rome in 2008 most backed an Etruscan wolf, and a 2025 study of the metal that points to medieval sources is contested too.

slides.prompt: The bronze she-wolf of Rome was long dated to about 480 BC. What did radiocarbon dating of the clay left inside her show?
slides.answer: She was cast between AD 1021 and 1153
slides.detail: 34 organic samples from her clay core, measured at the University of Salento, point to the 11th or 12th century, some 1,500 years later.

slides.alt: Animation in bronze and lamplight: the Capitoline she-wolf, a lost-wax mould in section with its clay core, an ancient statue in pieces beside the one-piece wolf and a bell, a carbon-14 decay curve, crystal traps filling and glowing, and a timeline from 600 BC to today.

slides.prompt: Slide the carbon-14 left in a sample. How much would a clay core cast in Etruscan times, about 480 BC, still hold?
slides.takeaway: About 74%. The wolf’s cores hold about 89%, 963 radiocarbon years, which calibrated against tree rings means AD 1021–1153, some fifteen centuries after the Etruscans.

slides.alt: Photograph of the dark bronze she-wolf standing on a stone base, head turned with ears up and mouth open, curls of fur on her neck; two small bronze boys kneel under her, looking up to suckle.
slides.caption: The Capitoline she-wolf, 75 cm high, with the twins Romulus and Remus added in the 15th century.

slides.heading: Five centuries of a dating dispute

events.text: Moved to the Capitol by Pope Sixtus IV
Restored; found cast in one piece

slides.heading: Two clocks in the clay core

left.label: Radiocarbon
left.text: Dates the organic remains mixed into the core, from the carbon-14 left in them: AD 1021–1153.

right.label: Thermoluminescence
right.text: Dates the clay’s last heating, the casting, from the radiation dose it has stored since: 8th–14th century.

slides.question: Why did the she-wolf being cast in one piece hint that she is medieval?
options: Ancient big bronzes came in parts
slides.explanation: Greek and Roman bronzes were usually cast in several pieces and joined. Casting in one piece was common in the Middle Ages, for bells, for example.
